sources.title: The U.S. debt tops a record-shattering $40 trillion (NPR)
U.S. government debt passes $40 trillion, more than doubling in a decade (CNBC)
US debt hits $40 trillion: Who does Washington owe? (Al Jazeera)
US debt hits 40 trillion dollars: the price per American (video, CNN)

chunks.text: The United States government has never [[owed]] this much money. Its [[debt]] has been {{piling up}} for [[decades]], and in August it passed 40 [[trillion]] dollars for the first time. Divide that by [[every man, woman, and child]] in the country, and it {{works out to}} more than 115,000 dollars each. The [[pace]] is {{speeding up}}, too: the last trillion arrived in only about five months.

verbs.correct: To grow into a large amount
verbs.wrong: To be counted one more time
verbs.why: Pile up means to grow steadily into a very large amount over time. The government's debt has been piling up for decades and just passed 40 trillion dollars.

verbs.correct: To equal after the math is done
verbs.wrong: To round down to a lower number
verbs.why: Work out to means to equal a certain amount once you do the math. This giant debt works out to about 115,000 dollars for each person in America.
Speed up means to happen faster than before, at a quicker pace. The nation's debt growth is speeding up too: the most recent trillion arrived in only five months.

chunks.text: How does a country build a debt like that? Every year, the government {{takes in}} far less in [[taxes]] than it spends, and the [[gap]] is now more than two trillion dollars a year. To [[cover]] it, the government [[borrows]], and borrowed money is never free. The government must now {{set aside}} more than one trillion dollars from its [[budget]] every year just to pay [[interest]] on the old debt.

verbs.why: Take in means to receive money as income, especially for a government or a business. Each year the government takes in far less in taxes than it spends.

verbs.correct: To save for one special use
verbs.wrong: To borrow at a lower rate
verbs.why: Set aside means to save a certain amount for one specific use, not for spending elsewhere. The government must now set aside over one trillion dollars a year just for interest.

chunks.text: Why should [[ordinary]] people care? Because heavy government borrowing can {{drive up}} [[interest rates]] for everyone else. When the government needs to borrow so much, families who {{take out}} a [[loan]] for a house or a car feel it too. The [[average]] rate on a 30-year US home loan is now near 6.7 percent, and [[long-term]] borrowing costs recently reached their highest level in almost twenty years.

verbs.why: Drive up means to force a price or a rate higher than before. Heavy government borrowing can drive up interest rates for everyone, including families buying homes or cars.

verbs.wrong: To pay a debt very slowly
verbs.why: Take out means to arrange to borrow a specific amount of money. Families who take out a loan for a house or a car feel higher rates too.

chunks.text: Experts from both political parties call the [[path]] [[unsustainable]], and, so far, the country's leaders keep {{putting off}} the [[hard choices]]. But the problem will not {{go away}} on its own, and the longer the country waits, the more expensive the [[fix]] becomes. In the end, the [[options]] {{boil down to}} spending less, collecting more in taxes, or both. [[One way or another]], someone will have to {{pick up}} the [[bill]], and it may be today's students.

verbs.why: Put off means to delay something until a later time, often because it feels hard. The country's leaders keep putting off the hard choices about spending and taxes.
Go away means to stop existing or disappear completely on its own. A debt problem this large will not go away by itself, and waiting only makes it worse.

verbs.correct: To reduce to the main choices
verbs.why: Boil down to means that many complicated choices reduce to just a few main ones. In the end, the options boil down to spending less, taxing more, or both.

verbs.wrong: To split a cost with others
verbs.why: Pick up here means to agree to pay for something, like a bill or a cost. One way or another, someone will have to pick up the bill for this debt.

mainIdea.s: The US government's debt has passed 40 trillion dollars, and it is growing faster than before. Interest costs are huge, and the bill may fall on future generations.
mainIdea.why: The debt hit 40 trillion in August, the last trillion took about five months, and interest costs top one trillion a year.

mainIdea.s: The US debt reached 40 trillion dollars, but leaders have already agreed on a full fix. New taxes and spending cuts will erase the whole debt within ten years.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no fix has been agreed. The article says leaders in Washington keep putting off the hard choices.

mainIdea.s: A large US bank lost 40 trillion dollars in a single day after a computer error. Customers rushed to move their savings before the stock markets opened again.
mainIdea.why: The article is about the government's total debt passing 40 trillion dollars, not about a bank losing money.
